the mechanisms involved in the induction of hepatic mixed-function oxygenases by various drugs.
the mechanisms involved in the regulation of drug-specific enzyme inductions.
the elucidation of the mechanisms involved in the induction of hepatic microsomal mixed function oxygenases.

the induction of aryl hydrocarbon (benzo(a)pyrene) hydroxylase activity in mouse liver requires both an initial increase in the cAMP content of the liver and an intact cAMP-dependent protein phosphorylation system.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the administration of inducers of mixed-function oxygenase activity to rats and mice results in an early and rapid increase in the activities or levels of cAMP-dependent enzymes.

a single dose of a chemical that induces microsomal mixed function oxidases results in an initial increase in the hepatic c-AMP concentration, followed sequentially by increases in the activities or levels of cAMP-dependent enzymes (e.g., protein kinase, ornithine decaboxylase, and RNA polymerase).
the induction of hepatic microsomal drug metabolizing enzymes is dependent on the induction of cAMP-mediated events, including hypertrophy, which is a prerequisite for enzyme induction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we found that cAMP-mediated hypertrophic responses in the liver are required for the induction of mixed-function oxidase enzymes.

cAMP-mediated hypertrophic responses are a common feature of drug-specific enzyme inducers, but that these responses are not required for the subsequent induction of micrososomal mixed-function oxygenases.
cAMP-mediated events appear to be a prerequisite for the induction of mixed-function oxidases.
